title: What God can and cannot do
source_text: Εἶτα ἀνθυποφέρει ὡσπερεὶ λεγόμενον ὑφ᾿ ἡμῶν τὸ δυνήσεται πάντα ὁ θεὸς, οὐδὲ τοῦθ᾿ ὁρῶν πῶς λέλεκται, καὶ τίνα πάντα ἐν τούτῳ παραλαμβάνονται, καὶ πῶς δύναται. περὶ ων οὐκ ἀναγκαῖον νῦν λέγειν, οὐδὲ γὰρ αὐτὸς. καίτοι γε δυνάμενος πρὸς αὐτὸ στῆναι πιθανῶς. ἔστη· τάχα μηδὲ παρακολουθῶν τῇ λεχθησομένῃ ἂν κατὰ τούτου πιθανότητι, ἢ παρακολουθῶν μὲν θεωρῶν δὲ καὶ τὴν πρὸς τὸ λεγόμενον ἀπάντησιν. δύναται δὲ καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς πάντα ὁ θεὸς, ἅπερ δυνάμενος τοῦ θεὸς εἶναι καὶ τοῦ ἀγαθὸς εἶναι καὶ σοφὸς εἶναι οὐκ ἐξίσταται. ὁ δὲ Κέλσος φησὶν ὡς μὴ νοήσας, πῶς λέγεται ὁ θεὸς πάντα δύνασθαι, ὅτι οὐκ ἐθελήσει οὐδὲν ἄδικον, διδοὺς ὅτι δύναται μὲν καὶ τὸ ἄδικον, οὐ θέλει δέ. ἡμεῖς δέ φαμεν ὅτι. ὥσπερ οὐ δύναται τὸ πεφυκὸς γλυκαίνειν τῷ γλυκὺ τυγχάνειν πικράζειν παρὰ τὴν αὐτοῦ μόνην αἰτίαν. οὐδὲ τὸ πεφυκὸς φωτίζειν τῷ εἶναι φῶς σκοτίζειν, οὕτως οὐδ᾿ ὁ θεὸς δύναται ἀδικεῖν· ἐναντίον γάρ ἐστιν αὐτοῦ τῇ θειότητι καὶ τῇ κατ᾿ αὐτὴν πάσῃ δυνάμει ἡ τοῦ ἀδικεῖν δύναμις. εἰ δέ τι τῶν ὄντων δύναται ἀδικεῖν τῷ καὶ πρὸς τὸ ἀδικεῖν πεφυκέναι, δύναται ἀδικεῖν οὐκ ἔχον ἐν τῇ φύσει τὸ μηδαμῶς δύνασθαι ἀδικεῖν.
pass_a_gloss: Then he raises as an objection (ἀνθυποφέρω), as though said by us, 'God will be able (δυνήσεται) to do all things,' not even seeing how it has been said, and what 'all things' are taken (παραλαμβάνω) in it, and how he is able. About which it is not necessary (ἀναγκαῖος) now to speak; for neither did he himself, although able to stand (ἵστημι) against it plausibly (πιθανῶς), stand; perhaps not following (παρακολουθέω) the plausibility (πιθανότης) that would be said against this, or following but also seeing (θεωρέω) the answer (ἀπάντησις) to what is said. God can, in our view, all things which, being able, he does not depart (ἐξίσταμαι) from being God and being good (ἀγαθός) and being wise (σοφός). But Celsus says, as not having understood (νοέω) how God is said to be able to do all things, that 'he will not wish (ἐθέλω) anything unjust (ἄδικον),' granting (δίδωμι) that he can also the unjust but does not wish. But we say that, as what is by nature (πέφυκα) sweetening (γλυκαίνω) by being sweet (γλυκύς) cannot make bitter (πικράζω) contrary to (παρά) its own sole (μόνη) cause (αἰτία), nor what is by nature illuminating (φωτίζω) by being light (φῶς) [can] darken (σκοτίζω), so neither can God do wrong (ἀδικέω); for contrary (ἐναντίος) to his deity (θειότης) and to all the power (δύναμις) according to it is the power of doing wrong. If any of beings (τὰ ὄντα) can do wrong by being by nature disposed also toward doing wrong, it can do wrong, not having in its nature the being-in-no-way-able (μηδαμῶς δύνασθαι) to do wrong.
pass_b_english: Then he raises an objection, as though we said it: “God will be able to do all things.” He does not even see how this is said, what “all things” are included in it, or how God is able. There is no need to speak of these matters now; for he himself did not take a stand against the saying, though he could have done so plausibly. Perhaps he did not follow the plausible case that could be made against it, or he followed it but also saw the reply to that argument. In our view God can do all things that he can do without departing from being God, from being good and from being wise.

But Celsus, as one who has not understood how God is said to be able to do all things, says: “He will not wish anything unjust,” granting that he can do even what is unjust, but does not wish to. We say that, just as what sweetens by nature, because it is sweet, cannot make things bitter against the one cause by which alone it acts, and what gives light by nature, because it is light, cannot make things dark, so neither can God do injustice; for the power to do injustice is contrary to his deity and to all the power that accords with it. And if any being can do injustice because its nature is fitted for injustice as well, it can do injustice since it does not have in its nature the inability ever to do injustice.

choices.choice: Copy-text: staged source_3.json section 70 (Koetschau 3.70). Celsus's words in quotation marks: 'God will be able to do all things' (δυνήσεται πάντα ὁ θεός), which Celsus puts in the Christians' mouths as an objection, and 'He will not wish anything unjust' (οὐκ ἐθελήσει οὐδὲν ἄδικον). The Christian saying recalls Gospel words such as Matthew 19:26 / Mark 10:27 ('with God all things are possible') and Job 42:2 LXX, but neither Celsus nor Origen quotes a verse here, so no inline citation is given. ὧν (staged 'ων') is the relative pronoun. παρὰ τὴν αὐτοῦ μόνην αἰτίαν is compressed; rendered 'contrary to its own sole cause', i.e. against the one thing that makes it act (its sweetness); 'by reason of its own nature alone' is a possible alternative. The last sentence states the converse: a being that can do wrong can do so because its nature lacks the inability to do wrong. 'Him/he' in the reply refers to God throughout.

'the answer to what would be said' to 'the reply to that argument' (τὴν πρὸς τὸ λεγόμενον ἀπάντησιν: the reply to the plausible case just named)

Recast the sweet/light comparison: 'contrary to its own sole cause' (calque) to 'against the one cause by which alone it acts'; 'by being sweet' to 'because it is sweet' (τῷ + infinitive, causal); 'nor can ... make things dark' kept as a second negated clause

Last sentence smoothed: 'by being disposed by nature to injustice as well' to 'because its nature is fitted for injustice as well'; 'the inability to do injustice at all' to 'the inability ever to do injustice' (μηδαμῶς)
No Scripture citation correct: neither Celsus nor Origen quotes a verse
